chapter_theme: Mullai: the wife waits through the rainy season; the evening, the thunder, the peacocks and the homecoming herdsmen each turn the promised season against her (15-24, 27-28).

15.reading: When the red-rayed sun has put away its heat, the green-stemmed jasmine smells sweet and the bees hum, she says that every time she sees the rain sky tossing with its clouds, her eyes toss with tears.
15.nuance: The two closing lines repeat one verb, அலமரும், for the sky and the eyes, and only the noun changes (காரோடு, நீரோடு): the sky's clouds and her tears are matched sound for sound rather than through a simile marker. The sun is not set but has 'hidden its anger', the cooling hour of mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain sky at the hour the sun cools, with jasmine in bloom

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which toss with tears as the sky tosses with clouds

16.reading: She tells her friend of broad, soft, bamboo-like shoulders that the man who left has not come, though the soft-stepping peacock calls and the lovely sky that drew up the sea has come with its lightning, and there is no one who asks her what is wrong.
16.nuance: The season has come (வந்தது) and the man has not (வாரார), and the last line turns from him to the household: her worst complaint is that no one even asks, so her grief is also isolation.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for the man who left while the peacock greets the rains

comparisons.tenor: the friend's shoulders, rounded and smooth as bamboo

17.reading: As the cool glory lily lifts its spoon-shaped buds to greet the rains and thunder roars in the high sky, the little evening comes like killers, so that those who have no one to hold them close tremble.
17.nuance: The victims are named as a class, புல்லுநர் இல்லார், 'those without someone to embrace them firmly', so the speaker counts herself among them without saying 'I'. The evening is called small (சிறுமாலை) and still comes as a killer.

thinai_evidence.note: evening at the coming of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the little evening coming upon those with no one to embrace them
the glory lily's buds, shaped like ladles

18.reading: As the sky scatters its swift rain and the konrai with pollen in its petals blazes like a growing fire, she looks at the lovely sky that seems to thunder as it spreads, and says her life seems to throb.
18.nuance: The two last lines rhyme இடிப்பது and துடிப்பது, each with போலும்: the thunder's beat outside is matched by the beat of her life inside, the same device as verse 15.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai's bloom under the first heavy rain

comparisons.tenor: her life, which throbs as the sky thunders

19.reading: As the peacock, longing for the raindrops, calls and spreads its plumes over all the woodland and dances, and this rain cloud thunders as if a pregnant one were bursting, she says her life seems to melt.
19.nuance: The peacock's joy and the cloud's fullness (சூலி, 'the pregnant one') are both images of fruition, set against her melting. Reading சூலி as the heavy cloud like a woman in labour is our reading of a compressed line.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock dancing over the woodland at the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rain cloud thundering as it breaks

20.reading: As the stags coming with their herd leap up, the jasmine twined with the creepers of the clearing puts out shoots, and thunder rolls, the little evening comes together with the storm, so that she and he both suffer.
20.nuance: யானும் அவரும் வருந்த: she imagines him suffering too, so the poem is not a reproach. The stags arrive (வரும்) with their herd and rejoice at the hour he cannot.

thinai_evidence.note: the herd of deer, the jasmine and the evening storm

iraicchi.act: the stags come in together with their herd at evening and leap for joy
iraicchi.sense: the beasts come home in company at dusk, which the man who left has not done, and so both of them suffer apart

21.reading: Before even the man who left her, letting her beauty fade, has come, the rain-fed jasmine shows its teeth, and the evening comes with the rain cloud to torment her: no one, she says, lives in such folly as we do.
21.nuance: The jasmine 'bearing teeth' is the usual figure for its buds, but next to her self-mockery it also grins at her. The closing line can mean that no one is as foolish as she, who still lives, or who let him go; the poem does not choose.

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine in bud and the rainy evening

comparisons.tenor: the jasmine's white buds, shown like teeth

22.reading: The herdsmen blow their konrai flutes and follow talking behind, the herd with its calves goes into the fold, and today, as she watches, the evening that comes every day has come, and the sky has thundered and drawn its bow.
22.nuance: Nothing is said of the man or of her pain: the evening is only watched (யாம் காண). The herdsmen and the herd coming home are a near miss for iraicchi; the act fits, but the poem never names the absent man, so the sense it would carry has nothing in the poem to attach to. The sky 'drawing a bow' arms the evening.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsmen bringing the cattle home at evening

comparisons.tenor: the rainbow the sky draws as it thunders

23.reading: As the frogs' clamouring voices and the bells on the garlands ring out and the roaring sky begins to rain, she asks whether her lover will fail to come today to comfort her when the rains set in, for her bangles will not stay on at all.
23.nuance: Whose bells ring (தார்மணி) is not said: cattle bells fit the mullai evening, chariot-horse bells would be the sound she hopes for, and either is possible. The slipping bangles are her wasting body's evidence.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains with frogs calling

24.reading: On the stony woodland, grown lovely, jasmine opens its buds on the bushes together with the wild jasmine; in the night the sky has stopped its tossing, the friend says, but the water of your kohl-lined eyes has not stopped running down to your breasts.
24.nuance: The rhyme அலைவற்று / முலைவற்று sets the sky that has ceased against the eyes that have not. The second half is compressed and our reading of முலைவற்று is doubtful.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony woodland in bloom after rain

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, still raining after the sky has stopped

27.reading: As the paandil of the rains smells sweet and the swarms of bees hum and dance with a din over all the woodland, the little evening torments her without mercy, never relenting, and, fighting it, her tears stand as they have always stood.
27.nuance: நீர்த்தின்றி, 'without fitness', makes the evening a wrongdoer; the closing line is obscure and we read it as her tears never ceasing.

thinai_evidence.note: evening over the woodland in the rains

28.reading: She asks her well-jewelled friend whether what has happened to her is like the pouring rain that lingers behind and then moves away, at the hour when the herdsman comes home wearing a fine garland headed with kurunthu flowers while bees hum.
28.nuance: The herdsman comes home garlanded at the very hour she asks her question, so his return frames her lover's absence. Reading the lingering rain as a figure for the man who stayed and left is ours; the line can also be read of the rain itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsman's homecoming with a kurunthu garland

comparisons.tenor: what has befallen her: the man who stayed a while and went

links.note: Both close on 'each time I see the sky' and the eye: Aimpathu 5 says drops mingle and fall from the eye (துளிகலந்து வீழ்தருங் கண்); Ezhupathu 15 says the eye tosses with water as the sky tosses with clouds (நீரோ(டு) அலமரும் கண்).
links.teaches: The shared closing formula could match eye and sky in two different ways, by substance in Aimpathu (tears are the rain's drops) and by motion in Ezhupathu (the eye tosses as the sky tosses), so the formula fixed the pairing but left the basis of the likeness to the poet.

links.note: Kural 1224: with the lover absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ezhupathu 17: as kodal buds and thunder greet the rains, the little evening comes like killers so that those with no one to embrace them tremble.
links.teaches: The Kural's image of evening as executioner, spoken by one woman of one absent man, appears in the Ezhupathu tied to the rainy season and widened to a class (those with no one to hold them), which shows the image was a mullai convention of the promised-return season before or beside its use as a private complaint.

links.note: Aimpathu 6: the bee humming at the jasmine is sweet to those who have someone to lean on, but the dark evening comes and saws at us who have no one. Ezhupathu 17: the evening comes like killers upon those with no one to embrace them.
links.teaches: Aimpathu 6 states both halves of the rule, sweet to the partnered and cutting to the lone, while Ezhupathu 17 states only the second, so together they show that the evening's cruelty was located in the hearer's state, not in the hour, and the later poem could leave the happy half unsaid.

links.note: Kural 1226: she did not know, while her husband had not yet gone, that evening brings sickness. Ezhupathu 21: before he returns, the evening comes with the rains to torment her, and no one lives in such folly as she.
links.teaches: The Kural names the woman's ignorance at the time of parting as the cause of her suffering, while the Ezhupathu's மடம் is a folly she still lives in now, knowing the evening, so the pairing separates ignorance that excuses from folly that the speaker mocks in herself.

links.note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is an envoy of the burning evening and a weapon that kills. Ezhupathu 22: herdsmen blow konrai flutes, the herd goes in, evening comes as she watches, and the sky thunders and draws its bow.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute the evening's envoy and weapon, and Ezhupathu 22, which names no pain at all, gives the same evening a second weapon, the rainbow drawn as a bow, so the reader of the Kural sees that the evening's arming was a scene the venba poets could show without comment.

links.note: Aimpathu 7: after the cattle have fed, the herdsman's glad flute at the red evening is like a spear thrown at her. Ezhupathu 22: the herdsmen's konrai flutes and the herd entering the fold are only watched, with no feeling stated.
links.teaches: Aimpathu 7 states the wound the herdsman's dusk flute gives, and Ezhupathu 22 relies on it unstated, so read together they show that by these short anthologies the homecoming herd and flute were enough on their own to signal the waiting wife's pain.

source_issues: Verses 25 and 26 are absent from our text, so the chapter has 12 verses for the span 15 to 28.
Verse 27: show flags that sangamtamil.com lacks this verse; its closing line is obscure in our text and the verse is marked uncertain.
Verse 19 line 2 பீவி looks like a misprint for பீலி (peacock plumes).
Verse 24 line 4 முலைவற்று is doubtful in sense; verse 28 line 3 படுமழைகொல looks like படுமழைகொல் with the final consonant misprinted.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses (the friend as addressee where none is named) and occasion words are null.
